episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Working Lands & Industry
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Working Lands & Industry.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: What gets lost when something gets easier?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down [Williams Lake Tribune] Grand Forks muralist nears 150 murals painted after Dolly Parton tribute and [Williams Lake Tribune] OPINION: Celebrating B.C.’s workers on Labour Day, plus 1 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Can AI copilots genuinely solve construction's labor shortage, or do they just make fewer workers more productive while obscuring whether local applications actually work? Topics include: Productivity claims versus reality: comparing vendor case studies to independent research on developer gains, Root causes of construction labor shortage: immigration policy and voluntary departures versus skills gaps, The role of friction in apprenticeship and tacit knowledge transfer in the trades, Rural digital infrastructure gaps and why connectivity-dependent tools structurally exclude parts of the Cariboo, The difference between testing tools at scale in San Francisco versus piloting them locally before broader adoption, Data ownership and institutional learning: who owns results if a contractor pilots NavigateAI and has to pay for access to their own performance data next season.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Agricultural Research Alliance

discussion.central_question: Can AI copilots genuinely solve construction's labor shortage, or do they just make fewer workers more productive while obscuring whether local applications actually work?
discussion.riley_position: AI copilots could provide real value by automating dangerous friction and guiding less experienced workers through tasks, but the actual productivity gains are modest (20-30% industry-wide, not the tripled-output claims in marketing), and nobody has tested whether these tools work on a Cariboo job site before recommending them locally.
riley_key_evidence: Faros AI found real-world improvement around 20-30 percent, nowhere close to tripling despite vendor marketing
Associated General Contractors' 2024 analysis: 54 percent of contractors report project delays caused by worker shortages, with 1.5-million-home shortfall tied to skilled labor gaps
Cover crops remain a durable agricultural fix precisely because they don't require connectivity, subscriptions, or platforms—proof that industry solutions don't always need technology
discussion.casey_position: The labor shortage is real, but likely driven by immigration policy and voluntary departures from the trades, not knowledge gaps, so an AI copilot only makes existing workers faster rather than solving the actual crisis; moreover, the apprenticeship model depends on productive friction and judgment that automation skips over, risking the loss of tacit knowledge foremen hold.
casey_key_evidence: Developer favorability toward AI tools dropped from 70% to 60% year over year despite increased use, and engineers are getting fired for not adopting tools fast enough—suggesting productivity numbers reflect coercion, not genuine tool effectiveness
2025 analysis shows shortage driven by sharp declines in undocumented worker inflows and accelerated voluntary departures, not a skills-transfer problem

Rural areas lack cellular coverage for precision-ag tools (20-30% without reliable connectivity), and rural residents are twice as likely to lack computers—meaning connectivity-dependent solutions structurally exclude parts of the Cariboo
discussion.resolution: Riley and Casey agreed to disagree on whether friction in apprenticeship is a teaching method or manageable risk, but unified around the central point: neither vendor metrics nor venture-backed promises tell us whether these tools work on actual Cariboo sites, and the only legitimate experiment would be a small-scale local pilot run by a regional trades program or community college, keeping a journeyperson mentor in the room alongside the AI tool to capture what it misses.
topics_covered: Productivity claims versus reality: comparing vendor case studies to independent research on developer gains
Root causes of construction labor shortage: immigration policy and voluntary departures versus skills gaps
The role of friction in apprenticeship and tacit knowledge transfer in the trades
Rural digital infrastructure gaps and why connectivity-dependent tools structurally exclude parts of the Cariboo
The difference between testing tools at scale in San Francisco versus piloting them locally before broader adoption
Data ownership and institutional learning: who owns results if a contractor pilots NavigateAI and has to pay for access to their own performance data next season
calls_to_action: Run a term-long pilot at a local trades program or community college extension where a handful of apprentices use an AI guidance tool alongside a journeyperson mentor—cheaper than a twenty-five-million-dollar venture bet and keeps experienced judgment in the room while there's still time to learn from it.

Anyone with experience trying a construction AI tool on a Cariboo job site, thoughts on cover crops versus precision agriculture, or knowledge of a foreman who reads timber stands by walking them should send that information to feedback@cariboosignals.ca so tacit knowledge is captured before it exists only in one person's head.

A Quesnel contractor or Williams Lake ranch operation could pilot an AI system on a single job at small scale and compare results against how the crew performed without it, generating local numbers instead of relying on vendor metrics.
